props.title: Who'll Stop the Rain
props.initialSlug: Vietnam vet smuggles heroin in deadly drug scheme

sections.content: Who'll Stop the Rain stands as one of the most compelling post-Vietnam noir thrillers, featuring Nick Nolte in a breakthrough performance as Ray Hicks, a Marine who becomes entangled in a heroin smuggling scheme. The film, adapted from Robert Stone's novel "Dog Soldiers," captures the disillusionment and moral decay of post-Vietnam America with the same raw intensity as Taxi Driver (1976) and Coming Home (1978). Director Karel Reisz brings his British New Wave sensibilities to this distinctly American story, creating a gritty atmosphere that influenced later drug-trade films like Rush (1991) and Light Sleeper (1992).

sections.content: The film's exploration of post-war trauma and moral compromise connects directly to other significant Vietnam-era films like The Deer Hunter (1978) and Apocalypse Now (1979). What sets Who'll Stop the Rain apart is its neo-noir approach to the material, blending elements of classic crime films with counterculture themes. The Creedence Clearwater Revival title song becomes more than just a soundtrack - it's a mournful commentary on the era's lost idealism.

The influence of Who'll Stop the Rain can be seen in later films dealing with drug trafficking and moral ambiguity, such as Traffic (2000) and Winter's Bone (2010). The film's unflinching look at corruption and betrayal established a template for how American cinema would continue to examine the intersection of crime, politics, and personal loyalty. sections.content: The film represents a crucial bridge between traditional noir and what would become neo-noir, sharing DNA with films like Chinatown (1974) and Night Moves (1975). Its influence extends to modern crime dramas that deal with military veterans in moral crisis, such as In the Valley of Elah (2007) and Hell or High Water (2016). The character of Ray Hicks became a prototype for the skilled but damaged veteran figure in American cinema.
